name: Evidence Extraction Tables
title: Evidence Extraction Tables
answer: Evidence extraction tables are structured summaries used in literature review and evidence synthesis to pull key claims, study designs, populations, interventions, outcomes and effect sizes from individual papers into a comparable grid. They sit within the AI Researcher section of the atlas and help a working professional move from a pile of PDFs to a searchable, sortable record of what each study actually found. The site's library currently holds 135 research papers and 11,222 claims extracted from research works, which gives a sense of the scale at which these tables operate.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables are structured summaries used in literature review and evidence synthesis to pull key claims, study designs, populations, interventions, outcomes and effect sizes from individual papers into a comparable grid. They sit within the AI Researcher section of the atlas and help a working professional move from a pile of PDFs to a searchable, sortable record of what each study actually found. The site's library currently holds 135 research papers and 11,222 claims extracted from research works, which gives a sense of the scale at which these tables operate.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The tables run on plain structured data, usually a spreadsheet or a database with one row per claim or per study and columns for source, method, result and caveat. They do not require a large model to be useful; a simple web interface or a CSV export is enough for most review workflows. Where automation is used, it typically sits on top of existing document parsing and text extraction pipelines rather than a bespoke inference stack.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by reading a paper, isolating the sentences that carry a finding, and copying them into the table with enough context to stand alone. Each row links back to the original paper, never to a secondary search tool such as Consensus, so the reader can verify the claim in its source. Extraction is usually done by a human reviewer, sometimes with a language model suggesting candidate sentences, but the final table is checked for accuracy and completeness.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on provenance and misquotation. Because each extracted claim must point to the original paper, the main risk is a claim taken out of context or a number copied with the wrong units or population. The site's practice of linking to the original paper rather than a search tool is a control against drift and secondary summarization. Reviewers should treat the table as a working index, not as a substitute for reading the source.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables are moving toward semi-automated population, where a model proposes rows and a human confirms or rejects them, and toward living tables that update when a new trial or preprint appears. The atlas's catalogue of 91 AI books, 805 scientific models and 732 AI tools suggests the surrounding infrastructure for such tables is already broad, but the table itself remains a human-readable artefact. The likely next step is better change tracking and versioning so a table can show what was added, removed or corrected over time.
